presentingComplaint: Sore throat, blocked/runny nose and dry cough for 3 days
history: Previously well 34-year-old software engineer, non-smoker, no chronic illness and on no regular medication. Woke 3 days ago with a scratchy sore throat that has become his dominant complaint, prompting worry about 'strep throat' as two office colleagues were recently prescribed antibiotics. Over the same period he developed profuse clear nasal discharge, nasal blockage, mild frontal heaviness, sneezing, a dry hacking cough and generalised aches. He feels warm but has not measured a high temperature. Symptoms are already plateauing on day 3, he is eating and drinking normally, and there has been no purulent nasal discharge, no facial pain worsening on bending, no 'double-sickening', and no drenching sweats. No dyspnoea, no pleuritic pain, no rash. No sick contacts with confirmed streptococcal infection; a young child at home has a 'cold'.
examination: Comfortable, well-hydrated, not toxic. Mild conjunctival injection and clear rhinorrhoea with congested nasal turbinates. Oropharynx mildly erythematous WITHOUT tonsillar exudate or tonsillar enlargement. No tender or enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes. Sinuses non-tender. Chest clear with normal vesicular breath sounds, no crepitations or wheeze. Modified Centor score 0 (age 15-44 =0, no exudate, no tender nodes, cough present, no fever >38C) - very low probability of group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

labs.note: Bloods not routinely required; obtained only to reassure worried patient - no leucocytosis, CRP not in bacterial range

imaging: None indicated. (No chest or sinus imaging warranted for uncomplicated viral URTI of 3 days.)
microbiology: Rapid antigen detection test / throat culture for group A Streptococcus NOT indicated (Centor 0). No testing performed. Illness clinically consistent with self-limiting viral rhinopharyngitis (rhinovirus season).
differentialDiagnoses: Streptococcal (group A) pharyngitis - argued against by prominent coryza and cough, absent exudate, no tender nodes, Centor 0
Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis - argued against by <10 days duration, no purulent discharge, no unilateral facial pain, no double-sickening
Acute bronchitis - cough is minor and not the dominant feature; chest clear
Allergic rhinitis / early influenza - no atopic history; lacks the abrupt high fever and severe myalgia of influenza
finalDiagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold)
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - The Common Cold / Rhinovirus Infections
ACP/CDC - Appropriate Antibiotic Use for Acute Respiratory Tract Infection in Adults - 2016
IDSA - Diagnosis and Management of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis - 2012
stewardship: Viral illness - antibiotics are NOT indicated and confer no benefit. Guideline-concordant management is symptomatic care only (analgesia/antipyretics, fluids, saline nasal irrigation, rest) with clear safety-netting. Modified Centor 0 means neither streptococcal testing nor empiric antibiotics are warranted. Counsel patient on expected 7-10 day course and self-limiting nature to reduce antibiotic-seeking.
contraindications: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics (drives resistance, C. difficile risk, adverse effects)
Avoid decongestant use in uncontrolled hypertension
Caution combining OTC products to prevent paracetamol duplication/overdose
edgeCases: Symptoms worsening after initial improvement beyond day 5-7 ('double-sickening') would raise acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
Persistent high fever, exudative pharyngitis or tender cervical nodes would prompt reassessment for streptococcal pharyngitis
Abrupt high fever with severe myalgia during influenza season warrants influenza testing/antiviral consideration
expectedMaiK: Recognise a self-limiting viral URTI (common cold) despite a sore-throat-predominant presentation that mimics streptococcal pharyngitis; the presence of coryza and cough with absent exudate/tender nodes (Centor 0) makes bacterial pharyngitis very unlikely, so no antibiotics and no microbiological testing are required.
expectedNextQuestions: Duration and trajectory of symptoms (improving vs double-sickening)?
Any tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes or high fever (Centor criteria)?
Presence of cough and coryza (features favouring viral aetiology)?
Any red flags: breathlessness, unilateral facial pain, drooling/stridor, or immunocompromise?
expectedInvestigations: Consider rapid strep test/throat culture ONLY if Centor >=2-3
Reserve chest imaging for signs of lower respiratory tract involvement
regressionAssertions: Engine should return URTI as top diagnosis
Engine should NOT recommend any antibiotic (viral illness)
Engine should not flag severity/admission criteria
PHARYNGITIS should appear only as a lower-ranked differential, not the primary diagnosis
No microbiological testing or imaging recommended for this uncomplicated presentation
